blocks.x: This is an interview on the 28th of June 1961 with Ed Kirkaby, who has been a booker in New York for many years, was the originator and booker of the California Ramblers, and I find that he has some acquaintance with New Orleans items, which I believe will make his story of interest to the archives of jazz music at Tulane University. Ed, what was your first acquaintance with New Orleans music? Where did you first hear a New Orleans group, do you think?

Well, the first New Orleans group that I heard was at Risenwebers, and that was the original Dixieland Jazz Band, which came up in 1917. I was with the Columbians, I said at the time, and I believe from the records, but my memory is very vague on the thing, that they made a couple of records for Columbia at that time, which for some reason or other were not put out. Victor finally signed them up, and the reception of the public was so great that Columbia tore its hair out and got after me, and got after me, who had an assistant manager's birth there, in charge of popular records, to get a jazz band together. So it was then that I turned to Earl Fuller, who had a Richter Novelty Orchestra with some very fine New York musicians in it at the time, and Earl also, and Earl also, by the way, had the Ted Lewis in a jazz band up in the upstairs after hours room, and it was to him naturally, I turned, and he came down, and I think that Earl Fuller's jazz band was the first jazz band records that Columbia put out.

It may have been the first jazz band that was derived from the New Orleans, the original New Orleans jazz band, too, was it? Do you remember anybody else imitating the original New Orleans jazz band style?

Well, we did make some records down there with Wilbur Swetland. He had a small combination, but the style to me, again, is vague. I haven't heard of Wilbur Swetland record since I left the company, which was in 1918, but those are the two, I was called jazz bands, bands that played jazz, let's put it that way, that I recollect of the Columbia, because in those days, jazz was pretty much of an unheard proposition.
Well, I don't know that this particular experience indicates that Victor was more enterprising, at least they were more...

Commercially minded, and they saw the fact that the original Dixie Land had rising members, was a terrific sensation. People could dance to the tempo, the two-beat tempo, and the result was that their business was fabulous. So, from a commercial sales aspect, the sensible thing was to get records on the market. And when Victor beat Columbia to the punch and got them on the market, why, they did a terrific business.
You bring up a point of great interest here. You think that the danceability might have been very important as far as the record was concerned.
Oh, I think so, yes.
Now, it wasn't just the novelty of the counterpoint and the conglomerate sound.

Well, oh, yeah, I think musically, I think musically, too, the band hit. It was something new and something that had a terrific lift, a beat as we call it now, and it, there it was. Before that, we at Columbia were using Prince's Band, making these 12-inch records of medleys, of tunes, which were supervised by the Hepburn Dance School at the time, to make sure that they got the proper one-step and two-step, not two-step, but foxtrot tempos, for which the records were sold, strictly for dancing. But it was not modern, not even up to the dance bands that were in the nightclubs, such as Rector's. And it was shortly after that that I began to plug, shortly after joining the company, began to plug for dance bands to come in and record, real dance bands. And Art Hickman, I think, was one of the first bands, if not the first dance band, that Columbia imported. And we had a terrific time recording it with both saxophones. And I know we couldn't take the banjos.
We mentioned that Earl Fuller worked for you for a time. How long were you with Columbia?
Ours was Columbia from 1914 to about 1918.
It was certainly during that time that the original New Orleans jazz band recorded at Columbia, but you don't remember it specifically.
No, that's very vague. They say that they made one date, which was not released at the time.
And it wasn't an audition record, because you were more or less in charge of that work.

I was in charge of test recording. That was new voices and new combinations that came in, you see, which we'd present to the committee, and the committee would judge them accordingly and appraise the possibilities commercially and go from there.
Well, then, they may have been engaged by the man who was in charge of all recording activities. Who was that?

Could have been. Could have been. They could have been sent on from a local dealer. There were times when artists came in to the auspices of local dealers for test recordings, which were handled by, say, the concert department or the international department, and maybe not the popular department, or maybe by one of the officials, the big officials themselves. That's how it's probably skipped by me, you see.
You would show material and suggest policy, and then somebody else would actually consult with the market people. That's right. That's right.
The committee would decide what to record.
And apparently this recording of the New Orleans jazz band wasn't brought forcefully enough to your attention until after Victor had made a success.
Then we heard the blow-up.
Yeah, yeah. You couldn't get them after that? No, that's right.
They tied up with Victor. But at that time, as I say, they started after me to get a jazz band to compete, and it was that time we...
Do you remember anybody besides Ted Lewis who was with the Earl Fuller?
Well, I think that the had... Earl Fuller, I know, played drums with the group, but who beyond that, I can't tell now.
Five or six pieces?
Yeah, I think it was the original... I think it was a clarinet, which was Ted Lewis, and a trumpet, of course, and I think the usual jazz band, trombone, and the drums.
Well, you were associated with a lot of jazz music after that. What was the next jazz band that you worked with?

Well, when I left Columbia, I went to the artist representation field, and I made records for many of the companies beside the big two, and I picked up the Memphis Five with Philly Napoleon and Mip Mole and Frankie Signorelli and the clarinet... Lytel with them? Bert Lytel. That was the trumpet. What is Bert's right name? Jimmy. Jimmy Lytel. Jimmy Lytel. Bert was the actor.
Bert was the actor, yeah.
That's right.
The drummer was... Was he Roth, the first drummer?
Roth, who is now with Jimmy Durante and has been with Jimmy Durante for many, many years.
Well, now Jimmy Durante had a jazz band. Was that at the same time? Was Jimmy Durante active in the period of the Memphis Five?
Well, Jimmy Durante, I think... Didn't he have this jazz band down in this place that he... The silver slipper that he and...
And earlier, a place called the Alamo, I think. Remember the Alamo? Which was far up north, uptown.
Jimmy Durante uptown? Yeah. May have been.
I think Kush has mentioned the Alamo as a place where he played with Durante and Baquet, and he thought that they were considerably imitative of the original New Orleans jazz band.
Could be. Could be.
I should say it would be. The Memphis Five, when you got them, had they recorded before? Do you think that...
No, I think I made their first date for them, and we then freelanced around. I think that the first date was for the Paramount Records, which was an independent company at the time.
Where were they located?

1140 Broadway. In fact, I auditioned the original California Ramblers down at 1140 Broadway in the Paramount. And, of course, I made records for them under Ananda Plume by the original Ramblers, with Red Nichols and Jimmy Dorsey and Tommy Dorsey, and, of course, Adrian Rilline, who developed into the greatest bass saxophone player in the world. So we had a real team at that time, you know, with great stars. And, as I say, I think I used about 20 nom de plumes or more. And I think that, as far as recording is concerned, I think I've, as an independent orchestra leader and production man, I think I've made more records than any other individual.
Well, I think more than any other man also, you've confused the picture for the jazz historian who tries to follow all the places you've been.

Well, I had a team of research men here for weeks looking over my records and diaries and getting personnel for these dates that I had on payroll books from 1925 or 1926 on, you see. But prior to that, it was simply the diaries. I've got the diaries from 1919 on, you see. And they had a real holiday and field day. I understand that those are coming out in discography form in the various issues of magazines from time to time.
The record research. The record research, actually. You used mainly the New York men, didn't you?
Yes, yes. I don't remember any New Orleans men. We had a lot of good men in New York that were influenced greatly by the Harlem bands, you know.
Oh, of course, yes.

Of course, our band, the boys used to, after getting off the California Ramblers Inn date, they used to hobnob down at the Nest, which was a famous nightclub. They had a big band down there, you know. And that's where they got a lot of their inspiration for jazz.

Yes, these fellows seemed to have great respect for each other. Even the non-jazz players used to visit Ellington and used to visit the Harlem bands to hear the tremendous sound they were producing. But just to step back again to the early years, do you remember what the name of the first record was that you made with the Memphis Five?
Now you've got me. I'd have to look that up.
Do you think the Sheik might have been the first record?
No, the Sheik was the California Ramblers.
Oh, the Sheik was the California Ramblers. That's right. All right.
But the funny part of it is, I had Philly Napoleon in that band.
Oh, yes. That's where I confused. You had Napoleon with the California Ramblers on that first Ramblers record. On the date. That's it.
On the date for Aeolian.
Yeah. Now, in the earlier records of the Memphis Five, you may or may not have been supervisor of recording and so forth.
I did. I think I made their first records and booker and supervisor of their dates for some time.
There's a terrific string of records of the Memphis Five.
That's right. That's right. That's right.
The Louisiana Five came along, too, in these later years. Yeah. That is, in the early 20s. They're late with respect to New Orleans jazz band. Did they work in the same idiom, same type of job?
Same type thing, yeah, sure. Same type thing. Philly, Napoleon, the gang, is Memphis Five. They worked up at the Healy's Balconnades. It was one of their jobs when I had them, you know.
Okay.
And, uh...
You said that was on 66th?

66th and Broadway, yeah. Lincoln Square, I think they called it. And, uh, that was a very popular dance hall, you know. And, uh, they really, uh, tore up the place there on Friday, Saturday nights, you know. It was a terrific business.
Louisiana Five had some New Orleans men in it, at least at times.
Do you happen to remember anything about that?
I don't, I had nothing to do with Louisiana Five.
Don't recall. Do you remember the name of Lada, Anton Lada? He was a New Orleans boy who worked with them.
What did he play?
Drums.
No, I don't remember.

And I think Nunez was with Louisiana Five on some recording. I'm not sure of the history of those people in New York City. They were with Louisiana Five at times, and I haven't run down very much information. Do you remember the names of any other groups that were in this category generally?
Jazz band?
Five, six, these jazz band.

Well, you know, we, when Nichols, Jimmy Dorsey, and Tommy Dorsey joined the Ramblers, we had a group called the Little Ramblers, of which I had Bill Moore, known as Jazz Moore, on trumpet. And we had Adrian Rillenny, of course, on bass. We used no trombone. Stan King was on drums. We had Jimmy Dorsey on saxophone. That was the first Little Ramblers. And, of course, when Reds and Red Nickel and our trombone, Tommy Dorsey joined, why we put them in, and, of course, we really began to get some real sound.
This is, in a sense, a big step in sophistication after the jazz band, New Orleans jazz band, wasn't it?

Well, we had built, what I had built, I had built the first big swing band with jazz men in it, you see? And that was my effort, you know, to build within the organization those men who could take off, who could play jazz. And we did it with what we call head arrangements. We would take a stock arrangement with no orchestration whatsoever, as far as special arrangements are concerned, and go into a studio, routine the thing there, by giving this man a break, another man a 16 bars and an 8 bar release, or a duet here, a duet there, you know? And it was strictly head arrangement. And all of the Little Rambler stuff was that way. The Goofers Five on OK, the Five Birmingham Babies, that was another OK combination of mine, but all the same men, you know? But they're all head arrangements.
You call them head arrangements, but to make an arrangement of that sort of work means that

the men have to be up to the capability. That's right. Well, don't forget my men had done more recording than any other white group and colored group to that time by recording for all these companies, you see. And my experience with Columbia Company and production and balance and also my musical knowledge and the knowledge of jazz beat and so forth made it possible to go out and turn out those sides, that number of sides.

Well, the New Orleans nucleus of good hot men, an all-star small cast, may have started out with the original New Orleans jazz band, then in various forms. We've seen it frequently thereafter. You talked about the Memphis Five. But then after you got the big band, you found that there was also a great appeal in having a small nucleus of stars.
That's right.
Do a performance in the small band since.

That's right. That's right. We had, as I say, we had Red Nichols. We had Tommy Dorsey on trombone. We had Jimmy Dorsey on Elder Saxon clarinet. We had Adrian Linney on bass. We had Stan King on drums, all of whom were soloists.
And Brodsky.

And Brodsky on piano. All fine, superb musicians who could... In fact, that band was known to the music publishers, which is a great tribute, as the band for the okaying of their arrangements. They'd come up with a manuscript, and the boys would put it on the stand and read it and knock it right off. No rehearsal whatsoever. That's a band that can do that, you know. No rehearsal. And then we'd cut it up, and we'd take solo parts here and give it to Red. We'd make a modulation here for Rilini, and ideas would multiply. And the first thing you know, you had a terrific jazz content within the arrangement.

This was about ten years after the original Dixieland jazz band played New York, or seven or eight years anyway. And by this time, the boys had begun to either get other influences or show a great deal of originality. They were using the original New Orleans jazz as a background, but they were beginning to show a little independence on phrasing.

Yes, they were evolving. They were evolving. Don't forget the old stuff was kind of raw, and very few people could play it, you know? Certainly the New Yorkers. Yes. And I picked up a fellow by the name of Bill Moore, who was a mulatto, and really was the first Negro musician to play in a white band, a big white swing band. Benny Goodman claims that prestige, but it's not so.
The Rams beat it by ten years. Well, I mentioned Durante, and Durante had baquet, so there's another case of a mixed band.
I'm talking about a big swing band.
In early years.
Oh, I think that down New Orleans, I'm sure, there was a mixture of musicians. It's bound to be.
Now, you mentioned Stan King, the drummer, and you said he didn't actually do much drumming in the studios. The early acoustical recordings couldn't stand for bass drumming.

That's right. We never, I don't believe, even when an electrical recording came, and we made the first electrical session for Columbia in Columbus Circle. And I remarked at the time what a different setup was going to mean in comfort and ease of operation as far as balance and isolation of solo parts and things like that was concerned. And we were very much intrigued by the fact that the drums, which we couldn't get before, even as far as snares are concerned, you know, we began getting that thing. But I don't believe we ever used a drum, a bass drum, until years later, when Reds and the rest of them had gone to other fields.

I imagine this holds for almost all recording studios. I've heard the story before in New York. And unfortunately then, we couldn't know all about the rhythm section of these New Orleans bands. Did Stan, besides being a very exact metronome, did he have any tricks that you recall? Any drumming?

Well, Stan King had a terrific rock beat. He was in, funny thing, he came from Hartford, Connecticut, you know. And you hardly think that a boy without some New York influence or Harlem influence, you know, would be able to drum the way he did. But I think he was the first one to use the press roll.
Well, that's interesting. The first one in the big bands around there.

The big band field, he used the press roll. And he was steady as a rock. He's the one that gave us our fundamental beat. Of course, he, Rolini and Brodsky, between the three of them as a rhythm section, were great. And we, of course, were far from attempting to create pure jazz. We used kazoos and every other instrument in the way of a novelty. We even put on a record with Rolini, playing it as a flute, instead of the pseudo-saxophone it was supposed to be, a thing called the coenophone. And I said, the recorder asked me what it was. I said, well, I said, it's coenophone. He said, geez, that's a word, isn't it? I said, sure. I said, from now it's the goofus. And that's where I coined the word, and that's where the goofus five came from. I see. The name of the goofus five.
Well, this isn't too different from what the New Orleans boys had already found out about using novelty instruments, washboards, and so forth. Yeah. That have a great visual appeal.

It came fundamentally from the Negro, you know, the Negro street bands, you see. But the idea was to get a novelty in the record, you know, and we might use it only for 16 bars, or say, what we call a break course, 16, 8, and 8. Why, it kept us spending plenty of money for imports of coenophones from France. Because they go out of tune very quickly.

I see. Yeah. Well, this, combining good jazz with commercial appeal, I think it deserves a great deal of attention. And you're being manager of the band, give you a little time to think about some of these things.

I'll say so. Well, the evolution of jazz in New York, you know, covers a big field. And when I joined Victor, as a manager of autism repertoire in 1935, my job then was to, to sort of lean over backward, to see if the, those people who were jazz minded, couldn't get more product. And it was then that I began bringing in bands in the Victor, for instance, Adrian Malini came in with a group, and he was playing at the Hickory House, not the Hickory House, but the, this, the present hotel. He had a little joint down there, and he had Fats Waller as pianist, in the, in, in the place. And, uh, uh, we called it, Adrian Malini, and just tap room gang. Adrian Malini and his tap room gang. So, uh, that's, uh, we made some records of Adrian, and, uh, and his tap room gang. Then, then we brought in, uh, uh, Joe Marcella, and, uh, made up a lot of groups, uh, to cater to the, the ever-growing demand for, for jazz records.
Well, you were closely associated with Fats later. Is that where you,

Well, uh, I went, uh, following Victor, uh, I went with, uh, the, uh, National Broadcasting Company, Consolidated Radio Artists, which was the band booking division. And we handled, uh, uh, Whiteman, and, uh, uh, Koo Kat, and, uh, we had, uh, Guy Lombardo, and, and Benny Goodman. In fact, it was, uh, during my regime at, uh, Victor, uh, that Benny Goodman broke wide open. I gave him the tune that broke him wide open. That was the Stomping at the Savoy. And, uh, he was making this tour, and, uh, well, the orders poured in for that record, you know, and, uh, Benny Goodman was, uh, King of Swing. So, uh, that's, uh, uh, but, uh, it was, and it was there, by the way, that, uh, uh, Nick LaRocca, and the old, uh, uh, Dixieland Jazz Band, formed a big organization with the little organization within it. And, you know who band the big one was?
Was it a previously organized group?
Well, they organized it. They did. It was,
it was the original Dixieland Jazz Band organized their own big band.

That's right. And they, uh, remember that, uh, they, they came to, uh, to, uh, consolidate Radio Waters because of its NBC connection, uh, to, uh, for booking. But it was not a successful organization. It was not successful.
They were quite successful with a theater tour. Now, they, they didn't take the big band?
I don't think they took the big band with a theater tour. I don't think so. That's vague. Now, I wouldn't, we, I wouldn't swear.
I saw them on the, uh, at the Orpium Theater in, or Riverside, I think it's called, Riverside Theater in Milwaukee, Orpium Circle.
They had the big band?
And they had only the small band.
That's right.
And it was a local band that played in the pit.
I think so.
uh,
I think the big band was not, was unsuccessful. We couldn't sell it for the money. That was necessary. I'm pretty sure.
You tried records, both with the big band and with the small band only.
I think, uh, Mills made some, some records. He was associated with us at that time. He had Duke Ellington and Cab Calloway. He's personal management. Yeah.
Well, the big band.
And Chick Webb, by the way, out of which, uh, Elder Fitzgerald came, you know, at that time. Great band. Great little band.
Uh, the, uh, uh, big band records of the, revived. Thank you.

New Orleans Jazz Band, were mainly commercial titles. So they tried to sell the big band on dance work and commercial titles and songs. Current titles, current songs. Yes, and the small band played the original repertoire. Yeah. You don't recall anybody in the big band?

No, I do not. No, I do not. We had so many bands that day that personnel didn't enter in. It was a matter of getting jobs. We were concerned with. When I took over Fats in 1938, that was the job of the lifetime. Because if ever there was a hunk of talent weighing 285 pounds, who was a genius without doubt, but who at the same time loved to have a good time, like any other mother's favorite son, I'm telling you that I spent six years of glorious listening and a great deal of mental turpitude and harassment until the sad day occurred, you know, when the body can no longer take it and Fats passed on in that train when we were coming in from Hollywood, California, 1943, December 15th. But during that period of his life in the musical business, he not only played for every type of audience, and I think we were the first ones to do the first jazz concert, strictly jazz concert out in Seattle for Norm Bobrow way back in 1942. Thank you.

segments.chapter: Columbia and the first jazz bands
segments.title: Hearing the Original Dixieland Jazz Band; Columbia turns to Earl Fuller
segments.summary: Kirkeby first heard New Orleans jazz via the Original Dixieland Jazz Band in 1917. Columbia, beaten by Victor, had him assemble a jazz band, so he used Earl Fuller's group and Wilbur Sweatman's small combination.

segments.chapter: Columbia and the first jazz bands
segments.title: Why jazz records sold: danceability, and Art Hickman
segments.summary: Kirkeby thinks the dance tempo and the new beat drove sales. Before that Columbia made dance-school medleys with Prince's Band, and he pushed for real dance bands such as Art Hickman's.

segments.chapter: Columbia and the first jazz bands
segments.title: Kirkeby's Columbia job and the unreleased Dixieland session
segments.summary: He was at Columbia 1914-18, in charge of test recordings, and explains how a committee chose what to record and why the Dixieland date slipped past him. He also recalls the Earl Fuller band's makeup.

segments.title: Forming the Memphis Five; Jimmy Lytell, Roth, and Durante's Alamo band
segments.summary: After Columbia he went into artist representation and picked up the Memphis Five. They sort out Jimmy Lytell from the actor Bert Lytell, the drummer who later worked with Durante, and Durante's Alamo jazz band.

segments.title: First Memphis Five date, Paramount, and the California Ramblers
segments.summary: He made the Memphis Five's first date for Paramount, auditioned the California Ramblers there, and recorded them under about twenty pseudonyms. He mentions his diaries and the Harlem Nest club's influence.

segments.title: The first Memphis Five record and The Sheik
segments.summary: Kirkeby cannot name the first Memphis Five record. The Sheik was a California Ramblers side with Phil Napoleon on an Aeolian date, and he supervised and booked the Memphis Five for some time.

segments.title: Memphis Five at Healy's Balconnades; the Louisiana Five
segments.summary: The Memphis Five played the popular Healy's Balconnades at 66th and Broadway. Kirkeby had nothing to do with the Louisiana Five and does not recall Anton Lada or Nunez.

segments.title: The Little Ramblers and head arrangements
segments.summary: With Nichols and the Dorseys the Little Ramblers formed, which Kirkeby calls the first big swing band with jazz men. They worked up head arrangements in the studio on stock charts.

segments.title: Small-band stars and Bill Moore as first Black player in a white band
segments.summary: The Ramblers' soloists could read-and-play with no rehearsal and publishers used them to okay arrangements. Kirkeby claims Bill Moore was the first Black musician in a big white band, before Goodman.

segments.title: Stan King's drumming, early electrical recording, and the goofus
segments.summary: Acoustic recording could not take bass drums, and Stan King's press roll anchored the rhythm. Kirkeby recounts novelty instruments, Rollini's coenophone and coining the name Goofus Five.

segments.title: Managing Victor's jazz repertoire in 1935; Rollini's tap room gang
segments.summary: At Victor from 1935 he brought in jazz-minded groups, including Adrian Rollini's tap room gang with Fats Waller at the piano.

segments.title: Consolidated Radio Artists, Goodman, and the Dixieland Jazz Band big band
segments.summary: At NBC's Consolidated Radio Artists he handled Whiteman, Lombardo and Goodman, and Kirkeby says he gave Goodman Stomping at the Savoy. Nick LaRocca's unsuccessful big band, Mills's Ellington and Calloway, and Chick Webb come up.

segments.title: Managing Fats Waller, 1938-43
segments.summary: He took over Fats Waller in 1938 and recalls six years with him until Fats died on the train from Hollywood in 1943. Kirkeby says they staged the first strictly jazz concert, in Seattle in 1942.
